home.title: A regular walk with a dog <mark>who's waiting for you.</mark>
home.lede: Walk a regular round with the dog of someone nearby who can't walk far any more, or with a shelter dog. Free, and always together the first time.
home.how1: Create a profile with a photo and say a bit about yourself.
home.how2: Choose a dog and request a first meeting. The owner or the shelter is always there.
home.how3: Hit it off? Then you can walk the dog on your own. The owner can see where you are, live.
home.how4: Go for a regular walk every week. Afterwards, tell us privately how it went.
home.forWalkersText: Time outdoors, a regular plan and a dog who's happy to see you. Aged 18 and over, free of charge.
home.forOwnersText: Can't walk far any more? You decide who walks your dog, for how long, and whether treats are allowed. Family can sign you up too.
home.forSheltersText: Put all your dogs online in one go, plan supervised group walks and get a regular group of young volunteers.
home.safetyTitle: Trust is built step by step
home.safety1: The first time, you always walk together with the owner or the shelter.
home.safety2: ID is checked in person at the first meeting. Rondje Mee doesn't keep a copy.
home.safety3: Solo walks are only possible once the owner has seen your ID in person and allows them for that dog.
home.safety4: During the walk, the owner can see live where the dog is. The route is deleted after 30 days.
home.safety5: After every walk, both sides give private feedback. Concerns go to our team, not to the other person.
home.safety6: You can always report or block someone. Anyone who breaks the rules is removed from the platform.
home.countriesText: We are starting in the Netherlands, around Tiel, Vijfheerenlanden and Gorinchem. You can already join in Belgium and Spain too, in Dutch, French, Spanish and English.
home.freeTitle: Free, and it'll stay that way
home.freeText: No ads, no subscription, and we never sell data. Rondje Mee runs on voluntary support, and later on partners and funds that stick to our rules.

quiz.title: Safety quiz
quiz.lede: Eight short questions about walking safely. No rush: each question tells you why, and one you miss simply comes back. After that you can ask for a first meeting.
quiz.passed: You can now ask for a first meeting or join a group walk.
quiz.failed: Almost. Take another look at the questions in red.

heat.q: It's 28 degrees. What do you do?
heat.a0: Just walk as usual, dogs cope well with heat
heat.a1: A short walk in the shade, bring water, and feel the pavement with your hand to check it isn't too hot
heat.a2: Have a good run, so it's over sooner
heat.why: In warm weather, asphalt can get hot enough to hurt paws. Hold your hand on it for a moment: too hot for you is too hot for the dog. Shade and water help.

leash.q: Can the dog go off the leash?
leash.a0: Only if the owner has explicitly allowed it, and only where it's permitted
leash.a2: Yes, if the dog listens well
leash.why: Off the lead only if the owner said so, and only where it is allowed. Even a dog that listens well can get a fright and run off.

treats.q: You have a treat in your pocket. Can you give it?
treats.a2: Only if the profile says it's allowed
treats.why: Not every dog may have every treat, for example because of a diet. The dog's profile tells you what is fine.

otherDogs.q: Another dog comes towards you. What do you do?
otherDogs.a0: Let them have a good sniff
otherDogs.a1: Keep your distance, ask the other owner first, and calmly walk on if you're unsure
otherDogs.why: Not every dog likes other dogs, even when it looks friendly. Keeping your distance and asking first avoids trouble.

escaped.q: The dog has got loose. What do you do first?
escaped.a0: Stay calm, don't chase or shout after the dog, and call the owner straight away
escaped.a1: Search yourself first, and only then call the owner
escaped.why: Running and shouting after a dog often makes it worse. The owner knows what works, so you call right away.

bite.a2: Make sure everyone is safe, exchange details, call the owner and report it in Rondje Mee
bite.why: Everyone safe first. Then exchange details, call the owner and report it, so everyone knows what happened.

stress.a1: It's not feeling at ease; find a quieter spot
stress.why: Yawning, lip licking and pulling away show that a dog doesn't feel at ease. A quieter spot helps.

overdue.a0: Let the owner know straight away
overdue.a1: Nothing, the app shows it anyway

hello.title: Saying hello
hello.sniff: You introduce yourself to a dog with your hand. Let him sniff calmly first.

first.q: You see Bobbie for the first time. What do you do?
first.a0: Keep your hand low and let him sniff
first.why1: A hand from above feels to a dog like something big coming at him.
first.a2: Pick him up for a cuddle
first.why2: Being picked up is scary for a dog that doesn't know you yet.
first.explain: Exactly! That way he knows who you are.

hello.ask: A dog on the street? Always ask the owner first if you may pet him.

away.q: Bobbie turns his head away when you pet him. What does that mean?
away.a0: Enough for now, give him space
away.why1: Turning away is a polite way of saying no.
away.explain: Well spotted. Listening to a dog is half the work.

body.title: Body language
body.signals: Yawning, licking lips and looking away often mean: I don't feel at ease.

space.why0: This dog is happy. Look at the eyes and the mouth.
space.explain: Yes. His eyes look away and his brows look worried.

then.why1: Crowds make it even more stressful for him.
then.why2: To many dogs a hug feels like being held down.
then.explain: Exactly. Calm helps more than attention.

body.whole: Wagging doesn't always mean happy. Look at the whole dog: eyes, ears, mouth and tail.

meet.title: The first meeting
meet.together: The first time, you always walk together with the owner.
meet.id: Bring your ID. The owner looks at it, {app} never keeps a copy.

bring.q: What do you bring to the first meeting?
bring.why1: {app} is free. Money never comes into it.
bring.why2: Treats only if the owner says it's okay.
bring.explain: Yes. That way the owner knows who is walking the dog.

solo.q: After the first meeting. When may you walk the dog on your own?
solo.a0: When the owner trusts you, has seen your ID in person and you passed the quiz
solo.a1: Straight away, you know him now
solo.why1: The owner decides. It goes dog by dog.
solo.explain: Right. Step by step, safe for everyone.

leash.q: May the dog go off the lead?
leash.a0: Only if the owner explicitly says so, and only where it's allowed
leash.why1: Even a dog that listens well stays on the lead, unless the owner says otherwise.
leash.explain: Exactly. When in doubt, he stays on the lead.

weather.title: Warm, cold and water

hand.text: Put your hand flat on the pavement. Hold it there for 7 seconds.
hand.after: Too hot for your hand? Then also for his paws. Walk on the grass or in the shade.

hot.a0: A short walk in the shade, with water
hot.a1: A good run, then it's over quickly
hot.why1: Running in the heat is hard on a dog.
hot.a2: A long walk in the sun
hot.why2: Sun and hot asphalt are too much for his paws.
hot.explain: Exactly. Short, cool and with water.

weather.salt: In winter, road salt stings paws. Give them a quick wipe after the walk.
weather.dark: In the dark? A light on the leash makes you both easier to see.

help.title: If something happens
help.sos: During the walk, the ‘Need help’ button is always at the bottom. There you'll find 112, the owner and what to do.

loose.q: The dog has slipped away. What do you do first?
loose.a0: Stay calm, don't run after the dog and call the owner right away
loose.why1: Running turns it into a game. Then he runs away faster.
loose.a2: Search yourself first, then call the owner
loose.why2: Call the owner right away. Together you'll find him faster.
loose.explain: Yes. Crouching down and cheerfully calling his name helps too.

bite.q: The dog bites another dog. What do you do?
bite.a0: Get everyone safe, exchange details, call the owner and report it
bite.why1: Walking away helps no one. The other owner needs your details.
bite.explain: Good. After the walk, you report it with the ‘Report’ button.

otherDog.q: Another dog comes towards you. What do you do?
otherDog.a0: Keep your distance and ask the other owner first
otherDog.why1: Not every dog likes a strange dog.
otherDog.explain: Well done. When in doubt, walk on calmly.

late.q: You're coming back later than agreed. What do you do?
late.a0: Let the owner know right away
late.a1: Nothing, the app shows it anyway
late.explain: Exactly. Letting them know is always good.

safety.title: How Rondje Mee handles safety
safety.lede: People don't hand their dog to just anyone. That's why we build trust step by step, and keep the platform clean.
safety.level1: New account: the safety quiz first. Then you can request a first meeting or join a supervised group walk.
safety.level2: After the first meeting: the owner has seen your ID in person and can allow solo walks for that one dog.
safety.level3: After that: request solo walks with owners who allow them for their dog.
safety.duringText: Your phone shares your location with the owner while the walk is on. If it runs over, you both get a notification. The help button shows you straight away who to call.
safety.afterText: Both sides give private feedback. Reports of an injured or stressed dog, or of someone feeling unsafe, go straight to our team.
safety.fraudText: Rondje Mee is free, so anyone asking for money stands out. Messages with payment requests, bank account numbers or links are flagged. Shelters are checked using their KvK, KBO or CIF number. Anyone who mistreats a dog or a person is blocked and reported where necessary.
safety.liabilityText: Rondje Mee puts people in touch and is not itself a party to the arrangement. The owner remains liable for any damage the dog causes and must be insured for it. We recommend that walkers take out their own liability insurance. Read the terms for all the details.
safety.reportText: Report it using the ‘Report’ button on a profile, dog or walk. We try to look into it within 24 hours.
safety.schoolText: Five short lessons about walking safely, about 2 minutes each. The first one works without an account.

perks.q: Do I get anything in return?

sponsors.a: Yes, if they stick to our rules: no ads in Rondje Mee, no data, and no say in which dogs or people are visible. A sponsor could, for example, pay for poo bags for shelters.

app.q: Why can I not contribute in the app?
app.a: Because money does not belong in the app: there, everything is about walking. Apple and Google also have their own rules for payments in apps. That is why you can only contribute here on the website.

about.title: A walk together, good for you and for a dog
about.lede: Rondje Mee connects young adults with dogs that want to get out more: from neighbours who can no longer walk their dog well, and from shelters.
about.metaDescription: {app} connects young adults with dogs that want to get out more: from neighbours who can no longer walk their dog well, and from shelters.
about.why1: Many young people love being outside and love dogs, but cannot have one themselves. At the same time, older people and people who are ill cannot walk their dog as often as they would like. And in shelters, every dog is waiting for one more walk.
about.why2: A regular walk with a dog is good for everyone: exercise, fresh air and a chat with a neighbour. Rondje Mee makes that easy, safe and free.
about.why3: Rondje Mee is not care or therapy. Not feeling well? The help page shows where you can turn.

how.meet: The first time, you always meet the owner and the dog together. Only after that may you walk alone, if the owner agrees.
how.adults: Everyone who walks is 18 or older and first takes a short safety quiz.
how.shelters: At shelters you walk in supervised group walks, at times the shelter chooses.
how.free: Rondje Mee is free. Nobody asks for or pays money for a walk.

walker.1: On warm days bring water, and feel with your hand whether the pavement is too hot for their paws.
walker.2: Let a dog sniff your hand before you pet it. That's how you introduce yourself.
walker.3: Sniffing tires a dog as much as running. A calm sniffing walk is a gift.
walker.4: Ears back and a low tail? Give the dog some space and talk calmly.
walker.5: In the dark? A light on the leash makes you both easier to see.
walker.6: Walk at your own pace. A dog that pulls learns more from you standing still than from pulling back.
walker.7: Sitting on a bench together counts too. Walks don't have to be fast or far.
walker.8: Another dog coming? Ask its owner first whether they may say hello.
walker.9: Walking in the morning? It's quieter and cooler then, nice for older dogs.
walker.10: Tell the owner something nice about the walk afterwards. It makes their day.

owner.5: A photo of your dog looking into the camera attracts more walkers than one from behind.
owner.6: Follow the walk live, or let go and read the report afterwards.
owner.7: Let the walker know you're happy afterwards. A thank-you keeps a regular buddy.

band.lede: Many people feel lonely or move less than is good for them. And many dogs could do with an extra walk.
band.adds: {app} adds something small: a regular walk with a dog who is waiting for you. Good for the dog, nice for the people around it, and a reason to get outside together.

page.title: Getting outside together, for people and dogs
page.lede: A walk with a dog is a small thing. Yet it touches on big ones: loneliness, moving too little, and dogs who could use more attention. That is why {app} exists.
page.metaDescription: A walk with a dog is a small thing, yet it touches on big ones: loneliness, moving too little, and dogs who could use more attention.
page.factsLede: Every figure comes with its source and year, so you can check it yourself.
page.mindTitle: Being outside, moving, and a dog who is happy to see you
page.mind1: Research shows that time in nature and regular exercise are linked to better health and feeling better. A little time with a dog is also linked, in research, to less stress in the moment.
page.mind2: A walk does not solve everything. It is a nice, regular moment in your week: getting outside, a chat with a neighbour, and a dog who is happy you came. That is what {app} is for.
page.notCare: {app} is not a care service and not a treatment. Not feeling okay? Talk about it, you do not have to do this alone.
page.suicideLines: Thinking about suicide? You can talk anonymously, day and night, with:
page.dogs1: Some people can no longer walk their dog as often as they would like, because they are getting older, are ill or find walking hard. Their dog misses the exercise, and they sometimes miss a chat.
page.dogs2: In shelters, dogs wait for a new home. A walk outside the shelter is a welcome change for them. With shelter dogs, you always walk in guided group walks on {app}.
page.dogs3: {app} brings these dogs together with young adults who love being outside but cannot have a dog of their own. Safely, step by step, and for free.

interviews.title: Interview questions
interviews.lede: For calls and visits. The questions are about what people did, not about what they would do.
interviews.rules: The rules: ask about the last time and about details, listen more than you talk, and only tell them about {app} at the end. A compliment is no proof; a meeting, an introduction or a dog online is.

shelter.title: Shelter
shelter.who: The volunteer coordinator of a shelter
shelter.goal: Goal: understand how walking is organised now and what is hardest. Listen first, {app} only at the end.
shelter.q1: How is walking the dogs organised now? How did it go last week?
shelter.q2: How many volunteers walked last month, and how did they find you?
shelter.q3: When did a walk or a volunteer last go wrong? What happened?
shelter.q4: How do you plan now who walks which dog when? Where is that written down?
shelter.q5: Which dogs get out too little now? Why those?
shelter.q6: Do you have a waiting list for new volunteers? What happens to those people?
shelter.q7: What have you already tried to arrange more walks? What did not work?
shelter.q8: Who decides about a new partnership, and what does that person need to see?
shelter.q9: How are volunteers insured during a walk now?
shelter.listen: A real problem is something they already spend time on, like a schedule or a waiting list. ‘Nice idea’ is not a yes; a date for a trial walk is. Write down the words they use themselves.

owner.title: Owner
owner.who: An older neighbour with a dog, or a family member
owner.goal: Goal: understand how walking the dog goes now, without selling anything. With family, ask about what they see.
owner.q1: How did walking the dog go yesterday? Who walked, and for how long?
owner.q2: When did you first notice that walking the dog got harder? What changed then?
owner.q3: Who helps with the dog now and then? How did that come about?
owner.q4: How often does the dog get out now, and how often would it really like to?
owner.q5: Have you ever let someone else walk your dog? How did that go?
owner.q6: What would have to happen before you let a stranger walk your dog?
owner.q7: How do you make appointments now: phone, WhatsApp, a note? Who helps you with that?
owner.q8: What do you miss most since walking the dog got harder?
owner.listen: Trust is the whole story: notice what someone needs to say yes (meeting first, a familiar face, family there). Never ask about money or an address. A warm reaction is not a dog online yet; a date for a first meeting is.

walker.title: Walker
walker.who: Someone aged 18 to 30 who loves dogs
walker.goal: Goal: understand what young people do now when they miss a dog, and what holds them back.
walker.q1: When did you last walk a dog? How did that come about?
walker.q2: Have you ever looked for a way to spend time with dogs without having one? What did you find, and why did you start or not?
walker.q3: What does a normal week look like? Where would a regular hour fit in?
walker.q4: What did you do the last time you wanted to go outside, away from your screen?
walker.q5: Have you ever volunteered? How did you start, and why did you stop or stay?
walker.q6: What would stop you from ringing a stranger’s doorbell for a dog?
walker.q7: Who around you has a dog that would like to go out more often?
walker.q8: How did you last hear about something new that you then actually started doing?
walker.listen: Notice the difference between ‘sounds fun’ and real behaviour (already searched, already helped). Question 7 often brings supply, question 8 tells you where to post.

vet.title: Vet
vet.who: A vet or someone at the front desk
vet.goal: Goal: understand when the practice sees owners who can no longer walk their dog well, and whether a flyer at the desk fits.
vet.q1: How often last month did you see an owner who could no longer walk the dog well? What was going on?
vet.q2: What did you advise that owner? What did they do next?
vet.q3: Who or what do you refer to now when a dog gets too little exercise?
vet.q4: What do you see in dogs that get out too little?
vet.q5: What is at the desk now, and what do people really take with them?
vet.q6: When did you last pass on something from a local initiative to clients? How did that go?
vet.q7: What would you need to know before referring an owner to a walker?
vet.listen: The right moment (after surgery, with an older owner) is gold: write down when that is. Ask whether you may leave a flyer, never promise a health effect, and never call the practice a partner without an agreement.

students.title: Student association
students.who: Someone from the board or a committee
students.goal: Goal: understand how members find activities and volunteering, and whether a group walk would fit.
students.q1: What was the last activity many members came to? Why that one?
students.q2: Do you do anything with volunteering or charities? How did it go last time?
students.q3: How do you really reach members: group chat, Instagram, newsletter, drinks? What gets read?
students.q4: Who decides about something new on the agenda, and when is it made?
students.q5: How many members had a dog at home? How do you notice they miss it?

p01.title: A dog is waiting for an extra walk
p01.sub: Walk a dog from your neighbourhood, for free
p01.goal: Announce: say honestly what you are building.
p01.caption:
I am building {app}: a free way to take a regular walk with a dog from your neighbourhood. Often the dog of an older neighbour who can no longer walk far, sometimes a shelter dog.

How it works:
• you are 18 or older
• the first time, you always meet the owner together
• after that you take a regular walk, at a time that suits you both

No ads, no subscription. {app} has just started, so you are early. Link in bio.

#dogs #walking #neighbourhood #volunteering

p02.title: Week 1
p02.sub: I am building a free app so grandma’s dog can go out more often
p02.goal: First market test: building in public. Comments tell you whether there is demand.

Week 1: I am building a free app so grandma’s dog can go out more often.

p04.title: No dog of your own? Fancy going outside?
p04.sub: Take a regular walk with a dog from your neighbourhood, for free
p04.goal: Demand: recruit walkers aged 18 to 30, in a city that already has dogs.
p04.caption:
Love dogs, but there is no room for one in your life (yet)? With {app} you take a regular walk with a dog from your neighbourhood for free, for example the dog of someone who can no longer walk far.

How it goes:
1. You make a profile (18+) and do a short safety quiz
2. You meet the owner together first
3. After that it is your regular walk

Walking together can do your day good, and for the dog it is a treat. Link in bio.

p06.title: Wanted: the first shelter
p06.sub: For guided group walks with young volunteers, for free
p06.goal: Partners: find a shelter, welfare organisation or university for the first pilot.
p06.caption:
I am building {app}: a free platform that connects young adults (18–30) with dogs that could use an extra walk. Dogs of older or ill neighbours, and shelter dogs in guided group walks.

Where it stands, honestly: the platform is live and the safety steps are in place (meeting together first, ID seen in person, consent per dog, a short quiz). There are no real pairs walking yet.

What I am looking for:
• an animal shelter that wants to try it with a few starter dogs
• a welfare organisation or neighbourhood team that knows older dog owners
• a lecturer or researcher who wants to help think about a simple measurement

Do you know someone? An introduction or a comment helps a lot. {link}

#volunteering #animalwelfare #community #socialimpact

p10.title: How we keep it safe
p10.sub: 18 or older · Meet together first · ID seen in person · Consent per dog · Short safety quiz
p10.goal: Trust: show owners and families how it goes, step by step.
p10.caption:
Letting a stranger walk your dog? Of course you think about that first. That is why {app} goes step by step:

1. Walkers are 18 or older and do a short safety quiz
2. The first time, you always meet together
3. The owner or shelter sees the ID in person (no copy is kept)
4. Only with consent per dog does someone walk on their own
5. During a walk the owner can follow along live, if they want

{app} never asks for money. Questions? Ask them below.
